title: Your first C program
goal: Write, compile and run a small C program, read gcc's messages, and know what gcc does to turn hello.c into ./hello.

topics.title: What a C program looks like
topics.examNote: On the exam you write C by hand. Every program you write needs `#include <stdio.h>` (if it prints), `int main(void) { ... }`, a `;` after each statement, and usually `return 0;`. Losing marks for a missing `;` or brace is easy to avoid.

blocks.text:
### Bash script vs C program

A Bash script is **interpreted**: when you run `bash script.sh`, the program `bash` reads your file one line at a time and carries out each line as it goes. There is no separate translation step, so an error on line 20 is only noticed when Bash reaches line 20.

A C program is **compiled**. *Compiling* means transforming code written in one language into another language. A *compiler* (we use `gcc`) reads your whole C *source code file* (plain text, usually ending in `.c`) and turns it into **machine code**, the language the computer's processor runs directly. The result is a separate file, an *executable program*, that you then run. If your C code has a mistake the compiler can see, you find out *before* anything runs.

| | Bash script | C program |
|---|---|---|
| you write | `greet.sh` | `hello.c` |
| before running | nothing (maybe `chmod +x`) | compile: `gcc -Wall -o hello hello.c` |
| you run | `bash greet.sh` or `./greet.sh` | `./hello` (the compiled file) |
| after editing | just run again | **compile again**, then run |

### The smallest useful program

This is the course's *Hello, world!* program, with every part labelled below.

blocks.caption: hello.c

blocks.text:
- `#include <stdio.h>` is a **preprocessor directive** (any line starting with `#`). It inserts the *header file* `stdio.h` into your program. That file *declares* `printf` and `puts`: it tells the compiler these functions exist and what they accept. Without it the compiler does not know them.
- `/* ... */` is a **comment**. The compiler ignores it. It may span many lines. Since C99 you can also write `// comment` to the end of a line.
- `int main(void)` starts the definition of the **`main` function**. Every C program needs exactly one `main`: the program starts running there. `int` means `main` gives back (returns) an integer. `(void)` means it takes no command line arguments. (The other form, `int main(int argc, char *argv[])`, accepts command line arguments; it comes on a later day.)
- `{` and `}` (**braces**) surround the *body* of `main`: the statements that run, top to bottom.
- `printf("Hello, world!\n");` is a **statement**: it *calls* the function `printf` with one argument, the *string* `"Hello, world!\n"` (text in double quotes). **Every statement ends with a semicolon `;`.** In Bash a new line ends a command; in C the `;` does.
- `return 0;` ends `main` and hands the integer `0` back to the operating system. You will see where it goes in the next lesson.

Spaces, blank lines and indentation do not matter to the compiler. We indent the body by 4 spaces so people can read it.

### printf and puts

Both are declared in `stdio.h` and both write text to *standard output* (`stdout`, the terminal unless you redirect it, exactly as in Bash).

- `printf("text")` prints **exactly** the characters you give it. To end the line you must write `\n` (backslash n, the *newline character*) yourself. Inside a string, `\n` is one character, not two.
- `puts("text")` prints the string **and then adds a newline itself**. It takes exactly one string.

So these two lines print the same thing:

blocks.caption: two ways to print one full line

blocks.text: Forgetting `\n` with `printf` glues the next output onto the same line. Here is a complete program that shows it:

blocks.caption: lines.c

blocks.code:
$ gcc -Wall -o lines lines.c
$ ./lines
onetwo
three

four
blocks.caption: real output: `puts("")` prints an empty line

blocks.text: `printf` can do much more: its first argument is a *formatting string* that may contain *conversion specifiers* starting with `%` (the notebook's `hello2.c` uses `printf("%s\n", "Hello, world!");`). You will learn those on a later day. For today, use `printf` only with plain text and `\n`, and do not put a `%` in your strings.

blocks.q: Which line ends a statement in C, and which ends a command in Bash?
blocks.a: In C a semicolon `;` ends a statement (the line break does not matter). In Bash the end of the line (or a `;`) ends a command.

blocks.q: Why do we need `#include <stdio.h>` at the top?
blocks.a: `printf` and `puts` are not built into the C language; they live in the C standard library. `stdio.h` declares them, so the compiler knows they exist and what arguments they take. The preprocessor pastes that header into your file before compiling.

blocks.text: Using single quotes for text: `puts('Hello');` is wrong in C. Text (a *string*) always goes in **double quotes**: `puts("Hello");`. Single quotes mean something different in C (one character), unlike Bash where both kinds of quotes make strings.
Writing `puts("Hello\n");` prints `Hello` **and then an empty line**, because `puts` adds its own newline after yours.

### Key points

- Bash is interpreted line by line; C is **compiled** into machine code first, and you run the compiled file.
- Shape of every program today: `#include <stdio.h>`, then `int main(void) { statements }` ending with `return 0;`.
- Each statement ends with `;`. Braces `{ }` hold the body. Comments are `/* ... */` or `// ...`.
- `printf` prints exactly what you give it, so add `\n`. `puts` adds the newline for you.
- Strings use double quotes.

topics.title: Compile, run, fix: the cycle
topics.examNote: Know the exact command `gcc -Wall -o hello hello.c`, what `-o` and `-Wall` mean, that `./hello` runs it, and that `return n;` in `main` becomes the exit status shown by `echo $?`.

blocks.text:
### The cycle

1. **Edit** the source file: `nano hello.c` (save with Ctrl+O, Enter; exit with Ctrl+X).
2. **Compile** it: `gcc -Wall -o hello hello.c`
3. If the compiler reports errors, go back to step 1.
4. **Run** the program: `./hello`
5. If the output is wrong, go back to step 1. **Every change needs a new compile**: `./hello` runs the old machine code until you compile again.

What the parts of the compile command mean:

- `gcc` is the GNU C compiler.
- `-Wall` turns on (almost) **all warnings**: messages about code that compiles but is probably a mistake. Always use it.
- `-o hello` names the **output** file `hello`. The argument right after `-o` is the name. Without `-o`, gcc calls the program `a.out`.
- `hello.c` is the source file to compile.

The order of `-o hello` and `hello.c` does not matter (the notebook writes `gcc hello1.c -o hello1`). The lab checker also adds `-std=c17`, which tells gcc to follow the C17 standard, the version of C this course uses.

Make a folder and your first program: `mkdir -p ~/cisc220_c/day1 && cd ~/cisc220_c/day1`, then `nano hello.c` and type the hello.c program from the first lesson exactly. Save, exit, then run `gcc -Wall -o hello hello.c` and `./hello`. Use `ls -l` to see that `hello` is a new file with `x` (execute) permission, just like a script after `chmod +x`.

blocks.caption: no news is good news: gcc prints nothing when there are no errors or warnings

blocks.text: Why `./hello` and not `hello`? Same reason as for scripts: the shell only looks in the folders listed in `PATH` for commands, and your current folder is not one of them. `./` says "the file in this folder".

### Reading a compiler error

Delete the `;` after the `printf(...)` line, save, and compile again. gcc 13 (Ubuntu) prints:

blocks.code:
$ gcc -Wall -o hello hello.c
hello.c: In function 'main':
hello.c:6:30: error: expected ';' before 'return'
    6 |     printf("Hello, world!\n")
      |                              ^
      |                              ;
    7 |     return 0;
      |     ~~~~~~
blocks.caption: a missing semicolon

blocks.text:
Read it from the left: **file : line : column : kind : message**. `hello.c:6:30` means file `hello.c`, line 6, column 30 (the 30th character on the line). `error` means gcc could not make a program, so **no new `hello` file is written**. The `^` points at the spot, and gcc even suggests the fix (`;`).

Notice the message mentions `return`, the next statement: gcc only noticed the problem when it reached the word after the missing `;`. So when an error makes no sense on its line, **look at the line before it**.

Fix the line (put the `;` back), save, compile again, run again. When there are several errors, fix the **first** one first: one mistake can cause a pile of follow-on messages.

Break hello.c on purpose, one mistake at a time, compile after each, read the line:column, then fix it: (1) remove the `;` after `printf(...)`; (2) delete the final `}`; (3) misspell `printf` as `prinft`. Compare what gcc says for each (the next lessons explain the third one).

### Warnings vs errors

- An **error** stops compiling. No program is produced (or the old one is left unchanged).
- A **warning** still produces a program, but gcc thinks something is probably wrong. Treat warnings as bugs and fix them; the lab checker shows them to you.

Example: this program declares an integer *variable* `x` (a named box holding an `int`, more on a later day) and never uses it.

blocks.caption: warn.c

blocks.code:
$ gcc -Wall -o warn warn.c
warn.c: In function 'main':
warn.c:4:9: warning: unused variable 'x' [-Wunused-variable]
    4 |     int x = 5;
      |         ^
$ ./warn
Hello
blocks.caption: a warning: the program was still built and runs

blocks.text: The `[-Wunused-variable]` at the end names the warning; it is one of the ones `-Wall` turns on. Without `-Wall`, gcc would have said nothing.

### return 0 is the exit status

In Bash, every command finishes with an **exit status**: `0` means success, anything else means failure, and `$?` holds the last one. A C program is a command too. **The value `main` returns becomes the program's exit status.** That is why a program that worked should `return 0;`.

blocks.caption: status.c

blocks.code:
$ gcc -Wall -o status status.c
$ ./status
about to exit with status 3
$ echo $?
3
$ ./status && echo ok || echo failed
about to exit with status 3
failed
blocks.caption: Bash sees status 3 as failure, so `||` runs

blocks.text:
- If `main` reaches its closing `}` without a `return`, it returns `0` automatically (special rule for `main` only). Writing `return 0;` is still the course style.
- On Linux only the lowest 8 bits are kept, so an exit status is always 0 to 255 (`return 300;` shows up as `44`). Use small numbers.
- `echo $?` reports the **last** command. Run it straight after `./status`, or you will see the status of whatever ran in between.

Compile and run status.c, then `echo $?`. Change `return 3;` to `return 0;`, run `./status` **without recompiling** and check `echo $?` (still 3: you ran the old program). Now recompile and check again.

blocks.q: You compile, get one `warning:` and no `error:`. Does `./prog` exist and run?
blocks.a: Yes. Warnings still produce the program. But read the warning: it usually points at a real bug.

blocks.text:
### Key points

- Cycle: `nano prog.c` → `gcc -Wall -o prog prog.c` → `./prog`. Recompile after every edit.
- `-o name` names the output (default `a.out`); `-Wall` turns on warnings.
- Error messages read `file:line:column: error: message`. If the line looks fine, check the line before. Fix the first error first.
- Error: no program made. Warning: program made, but probably buggy.
- `return n;` in `main` sets the exit status; see it with `echo $?`. `0` means success.

topics.title: What gcc actually does
topics.examNote: Be able to name the four stages in order (preprocessing, compiling, assembling, linking), say what each produces, and say which stage reports `undefined reference`.

blocks.text:
### Four stages

`gcc hello.c -o hello` looks like one step, but gcc runs four in a row:

1. **Preprocessing.** The *preprocessor* handles the lines starting with `#`. `#include <stdio.h>` is replaced by the whole text of `stdio.h`, and comments are removed. Your file plus the headers it includes is called a *translation unit*. Stop here with `gcc -E hello.c > hello.i`.
2. **Compiling.** The translation unit is turned into **assembly language**, a human-readable language whose lines map closely to the processor's machine instructions. Stop here with `gcc -S hello.c` (writes `hello.s`).
3. **Assembling.** The assembly is turned into **object code** (`hello.o`): machine code for *this one file only*. It contains a *call* to `printf`, but not `printf` itself. Stop here with `gcc -c hello.c`.
4. **Linking.** The *linker* (`ld`) joins the object code with the code of the functions it calls, here from the **C standard library**, where the machine code for `printf` and `puts` lives. The result is the executable `hello`. The standard library is linked automatically.

In your day1 folder run `gcc -E hello.c > hello.i`, then `wc -l hello.i` (over 800 lines from a 7-line file: that is `stdio.h` pasted in) and `tail -5 hello.i` (your `main` is at the end, and your comment is gone). Then `gcc -S hello.c` and `cat hello.s`: look for a line `call` with `printf` or `puts` (gcc may swap a simple `printf` ending in `\n` for `puts`). Finally `gcc -c hello.c` and `ls`.

blocks.caption: the end of the preprocessor output (the line count depends on your system)

blocks.text:
### Errors from different stages

Knowing the stages tells you what kind of mistake you made. Here `printf` is misspelled as `prinft`:

blocks.code:
$ gcc -Wall -o typo typo.c
typo.c: In function 'main':
typo.c:4:5: warning: implicit declaration of function 'prinft'; did you mean 'printf'? [-Wimplicit-function-declaration]
    4 |     prinft("Hello\n");
      |     ^~~~~~
      |     printf
/usr/bin/ld: /tmp/cc3XZNQe.o: in function `main':
typo.c:(.text+0x18): undefined reference to `prinft'
collect2: error: ld returned 1 exit status
blocks.caption: a compiler warning, then a linker error (the /tmp name changes every time)

blocks.text:
- The **compiler** only warns: no header declares `prinft`, but it lets the call through, hoping it is defined somewhere else.
- The **linker** (`ld`) then searches your object code and the standard library for a function named `prinft`, finds none, and fails: **`undefined reference to`** always means a *linking* problem. Note there is no line:column here, because the linker works on object code, not on your source text.

(Forgetting `#include <stdio.h>` gives a similar `implicit declaration of function 'puts'` warning. On our gcc 13 the program still links, because `puts` really is in the library, but newer gcc versions make it an error. Always include the header.)

### -lm goes after the source file

Math functions such as `sin` and `pow` (declared in `math.h`) are in a separate *math library* that is **not** linked automatically. You ask for it with `-lm` ("link library m"). You will need this for Assignment 4's `sin.c`.

**Where you put `-lm` matters.** The linker reads its inputs **left to right**. When it reaches a library, it only takes the functions that the files *before it* still need. If `-lm` comes first, nothing needs `pow` yet, so nothing is taken; then your file asks for `pow` and it is too late. On Ubuntu, with a file `m.c` that calls `pow` (the code itself does not matter today):

blocks.code:
$ gcc -o m -lm m.c
/usr/bin/ld: /tmp/ccyj9svi.o: in function `main':
m.c:(.text+0x3f): undefined reference to `pow'
collect2: error: ld returned 1 exit status
$ gcc -o m m.c -lm
$
blocks.caption: same files, different order: the second one works

blocks.text: The Assignment 4 handout writes `gcc -o sin -lm sin.c`. On Ubuntu that fails with `undefined reference to 'pow'` even if your code is perfect. Use `gcc -Wall -o sin sin.c -lm`.

Mixing up names after `-o` destroys files: `gcc -o first.c second.c` silently **replaces your source file `first.c`** with machine code. (gcc refuses only when the two names are identical.) Always write the program name, with no `.c`, right after `-o`.

blocks.q: Why does a typo in a function name give no line number in the final error?
blocks.a: Because the final error comes from the linker. The linker works on object code, after your source text has been compiled, so it only knows which function was missing (`undefined reference to 'prinft'`), not the line in your file. The compiler's warning just above it does have the line:column.

blocks.text:
### Key points

- gcc's four stages: **preprocess** (`#include`, remove comments; `-E`), **compile** to assembly (`-S`, `.s`), **assemble** to object code (`-c`, `.o`), **link** with the library to make the executable.
- Object code for your file contains calls to `printf`/`puts` but not their code; the linker brings that in from the C standard library.
- `undefined reference to` = linker error: a misspelled function or a missing library.
- The math library needs `-lm`, written **after** the `.c` file, because the linker reads left to right.

flashcards.front: Compiled vs interpreted: which is C, which is Bash?
flashcards.back: C is compiled: gcc translates the whole file into machine code, then you run the result. Bash is interpreted: bash reads and runs the script line by line.
A preprocessor directive that inserts the header file stdio.h, which declares `printf` and `puts` so the compiler knows them.

flashcards.front: Where does a C program start running?
flashcards.back: At the `main` function. Every program needs exactly one.
`main` returns an `int` (the exit status) and takes no command line arguments.

flashcards.front: What ends a statement in C?
flashcards.back: A semicolon `;`. Line breaks and indentation do not matter to the compiler.

flashcards.front: Two kinds of comments in C?
flashcards.back: `/* ... */` (can span lines) and `// ...` to the end of the line (since C99).
`printf("hi")` prints exactly `hi`, no newline; you add `\n`. `puts("hi")` prints `hi` and adds a newline itself.

flashcards.front: Command to compile hello.c into a program named hello, with warnings?
What does `-o` do? What if you leave it out?
flashcards.back: Names the output file (the next argument). Without it gcc writes `a.out`.
Turns on (almost) all warnings: messages about code that compiles but is probably wrong.

flashcards.front: How to read `hello.c:6:30: error: expected ';' before 'return'`?
flashcards.back: File hello.c, line 6, column 30, an error (no program made). The `;` is missing at the end of line 6, just before `return`.
Error: compiling stops and no program is made. Warning: the program is made but is probably buggy; fix it anyway.
It becomes the program's exit status; `echo $?` right after running prints 3.

flashcards.front: You edited prog.c but `./prog` still behaves the old way. Why?
flashcards.back: You did not recompile. `./prog` runs the old machine code until you run gcc again.
Preprocessing, compiling (to assembly), assembling (to object code), linking (to the executable).
Linking: no object code or library defines a function named xyz (typo, or missing library like `-lm`).
After the source file: `gcc -o sin sin.c -lm`. The linker reads left to right and only takes from a library what earlier files need.

quiz.explain: The first `printf` has no `\n`, so `cd` continues the same line. `puts` adds its own newline after `ef`.
`puts("")` prints only a newline, which shows as an empty line.
`puts` prints `x`, then your `\n`, then its own newline: so there is an empty line between `x` and `y`.
One `printf` can print several lines: each `\n` ends one. The two `puts` calls are inside comments, so they never run.

quiz.q: Which line correctly prints `Hi` followed by a newline?
quiz.explain: Strings need double quotes (not single), `printf` needs `\n` for the newline, and every statement needs a `;`.

quiz.q: In one or two sentences: how is running a C program different from running a Bash script?
quiz.answer: A Bash script is interpreted: bash reads and runs it line by line. A C program must first be compiled by gcc into a machine-code executable, and then you run that executable (e.g. `./hello`); after every edit you must compile again.
quiz.explain: Compiled vs interpreted is the key difference. The compiler checks the whole file before anything runs.

quiz.q: Write the command that compiles `pattern.c` into a program named `pattern` with all warnings on, and the command that runs it.
quiz.explain: `-o pattern` names the output; `-Wall` enables warnings; `./` runs a file in the current folder.

quiz.q: gcc prints `prog.c:5:5: error: expected ';' before 'return'`. What do the two numbers mean, and where is the mistake most likely?
quiz.answer: Line 5, column 5. The `;` is missing at the end of the statement before `return`, most likely on line 4.
quiz.explain: gcc only notices a missing `;` when it reaches the next word, so look at the line before.

quiz.q: You compile this as `prog`. What does `./prog; echo $?` print?
quiz.explain: The program prints `done`; `main` returns 2, which is the exit status that `echo $?` shows.

quiz.q: You compile this as `prog`. What does `./prog && echo yes || echo no` print?
quiz.explain: Exit status 1 means failure in Bash, so `&&` skips `echo yes` and `||` runs `echo no`.

quiz.q: gcc prints one `warning:` line and nothing else. What happened?
options: The program was made, but gcc thinks some code is probably wrong
quiz.explain: Warnings do not stop compiling. Errors do. A warning is still worth fixing.

quiz.q: Which gcc stage replaces `#include <stdio.h>` with the contents of the header?
quiz.explain: Lines starting with `#` are preprocessor directives, handled first. `gcc -E` shows the result.

quiz.q: `gcc -o area -lm area.c` fails with `undefined reference to 'sqrt'`, but the code is correct. Fix the command and explain why it works.
quiz.answer: `gcc -o area area.c -lm`. The linker reads left to right and only takes functions from a library that earlier inputs still need; with `-lm` first nothing needed `sqrt` yet, so it was skipped.
quiz.explain: `undefined reference` is a linker error. Put libraries after the source files.

write.prompt:
Write a complete C program `menu.c` that prints these three lines exactly, then ends successfully:

```
Menu
1. Soup
2. Salad
```

Use `puts` for the first line and a single `printf` for the other two.
write.explain: `#include <stdio.h>` declares `puts` and `printf`. The program starts at `main`. `puts` adds the newline after `Menu` itself. One `printf` prints two lines because the string contains two `\n`; the last `\n` is needed so the output ends with a newline. `return 0;` gives exit status 0 (success).

write.prompt:
Write a complete C program that prints this arrow exactly (no spaces at the ends of lines) and exits with status 0. Use any mix of `printf` and `puts`.

```
  ^
 /|
  |
  |
```

Hint: the second line is a space, a slash and a bar.

rubric.item: four lines exactly right, including leading spaces, each ending in a newline

pitfalls: a `/` is a normal character in a string, but a backslash `\` is not (it starts an escape like `\n`), which is why this arrow avoids it
